title: Zephaniah 2:1–15
context: Zephaniah 2:1–15 begins with the prophet calling a shameless nation to gather before the day of the LORD’s anger arrives, and urging the humble of the land to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility, for perhaps they will be hidden on that day. Oracles against the nations follow in every direction: the Philistine cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron to the west, whose coast will become pasture for the remnant of Judah; Moab and Ammon to the east, who taunted God’s people and will become like Sodom and Gomorrah; the Cushites to the south; and Assyria and its capital Nineveh to the north. The LORD will famish the gods of the land, and people from every shore will worship him. Nineveh, the carefree city that said, "I am, and there is no one besides me," will become a desolation. The book of Nahum also announces Nineveh’s fall; the two prophets are named side by side here without blending their messages. Nineveh fell in the late seventh century BC. Shared ground: both traditions read the remnant who seek the LORD as the humble faithful whom God preserves through judgment.

verses.text: Gather yourselves together, yes, gather together, you nation that has no shame,
verses.arminianNotes: Zephaniah calls the shameless nation to gather themselves together. Arminian readers see a call to assemble in repentance while there is still time, showing that God gives opportunity before judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the call as God’s gracious summons. Both traditions note that the Hebrew verb is unusual and read in different ways, and they hold the precise sense loosely.

verses.text: before the appointed time when the day passes as the chaff, before the fierce anger of the LORD comes on you, before the day of the LORD’s anger comes on you.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet urges them to act before the appointed time when the day passes like chaff and the LORD’s anger comes. Arminians see an urgent window for repentance, with judgment approaching quickly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the appointed time as set by God. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: there is a time to respond, and it will not last forever.

verses.text: Seek the LORD, all you humble of the land, who have kept his ordinances. Seek righteousness. Seek humility. It may be that you will be hidden in the day of the LORD’s anger.
verses.arminianNotes: Zephaniah calls the humble of the land to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility, for perhaps they will be hidden in the day of his anger. Arminian readers see a genuine call to the faithful to keep seeking God, with the hope of protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the humble as those whom God has preserved and who show it by seeking him. Both traditions note the word perhaps, which leaves room for humble trust rather than presumption, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: For Gaza will be forsaken, and Ashkelon a desolation. They will drive out Ashdod at noonday, and Ekron will be rooted up.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says Gaza will be forsaken, Ashkelon a desolation, Ashdod driven out at noon, and Ekron uprooted. Arminians see God’s judgment extending to the nations around Judah, showing his rule over all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the Philistine cities. Both traditions note that the Hebrew contains wordplay on the names Gaza and Ekron, and they read the verse as announcing their ruin.

verses.text: Woe to the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites! The LORD’s word is against you, Canaan, the land of the Philistines. I will destroy you until there is no inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet pronounces woe on the coastland and the Cherethites, saying the LORD’s word is against Canaan, the land of the Philistines. Arminian readers see the nations held accountable for their opposition to God and his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s word as effective against the nations. Both traditions note that the Cherethites were associated with the Philistines (compare 1 Samuel 30:14), and they read the verse as continuing the oracle.

verses.text: The sea coast will be pastures, with cottages for shepherds and folds for flocks.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the coast will become pastures with cottages for shepherds and folds for flocks. Arminians see the transformation of hostile cities into quiet pastureland as a sign of God’s reversal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God turning places of opposition into places of peace. Both traditions read the image as preparing for the promise to the remnant in verse 7.

verses.text: The coast will be for the remnant of the house of Judah. They will find pasture. In the houses of Ashkelon, they will lie down in the evening, for the LORD, their God, will visit them and restore them.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the coast will belong to the remnant of Judah, who will find pasture, for the LORD will visit and restore them. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to the remnant who seek him, giving them a future beyond judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the remnant as the object of God’s preserving grace. Both traditions hold the restoration of the remnant as shared ground, and they note that restore their fortunes appears again in 3:20.

verses.text: I have heard the reproach of Moab and the insults of the children of Ammon, with which they have reproached my people and magnified themselves against their border.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has heard the taunts of Moab and Ammon against his people. Arminians see God’s concern for his people, as he hears and responds to those who mock them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s defense of his covenant people. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note the long history of conflict between Israel and these nations.

verses.text: Therefore, as I live, says the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, surely Moab will be as Sodom, and the children of Ammon as Gomorrah, a possession of nettles and salt pits, and a perpetual desolation. The remnant of my people will plunder them, and the survivors of my nation will inherit them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies swears that Moab and Ammon will be like Sodom and Gomorrah, and the remnant of his people will plunder them. Arminian readers see God’s oath as making his judgment certain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the oath as expressing God’s unchangeable purpose. Both traditions note the link to Sodom and Gomorrah and to the origins of Moab and Ammon (Genesis 19), and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: This they will have for their pride, because they have reproached and magnified themselves against the people of the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says this will come because of their pride and their insults against the people of the LORD of Armies. Arminians see pride as the root of their sin, as they magnified themselves against God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God opposing the proud. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and compare the theme of pride in Isaiah 16:6 by reference.

verses.text: The LORD will be awesome to them, for he will famish all the gods of the land. Men will worship him, everyone from his place, even all the shores of the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the LORD will be awesome to them, famish the gods of the land, and people from all shores will worship him. Arminian readers see God’s judgment leading to worship among the nations, showing his desire for all peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the gathering of the nations as God’s sovereign purpose. Both traditions hold the worship of the nations as shared ground and read it alongside 3:9–10.

verses.text: You Cushites also, you will be killed by my sword.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the Cushites will also be killed by his sword. Arminians see God’s judgment reaching even distant nations to the south, showing that none are beyond his reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s rule over all peoples. Both traditions note that Cush was associated with the region south of Egypt, and that 3:10 later speaks of worshipers from beyond the rivers of Cush.

verses.text: He will stretch out his hand against the north, destroy Assyria, and will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the LORD will stretch out his hand against the north, destroy Assyria, and make Nineveh a desolation. Arminian readers see God judging the most powerful empire of the day, showing that no nation stands above him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the rise and fall of empires. Both traditions note that the book of Nahum also announces Nineveh’s fall, and they name the two prophets side by side without blending their messages.

verses.text: Herds will lie down in the middle of her, all kinds of animals. Both the pelican and the porcupine will lodge in its capitals. Their calls will echo through the windows. Desolation will be in the thresholds, for he has laid bare the cedar beams.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says herds and wild animals will lie down in Nineveh, birds will lodge in its ruins, and desolation will fill its thresholds. Arminians see a vivid picture of a great city reduced to ruins.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as showing the end of human pride. Both traditions note that the exact animals named are uncertain in translation, and they read the verse as a picture of total desolation.

verses.text: This is the joyous city that lived carelessly, that said in her heart, “I am, and there is no one besides me.” How she has become a desolation, a place for animals to lie down in! Everyone who passes by her will hiss and shake their fists.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says this was the carefree city that said, "I am, and there is no one besides me," yet it became a desolation. Arminian readers see arrogant self-sufficiency as the sin that brought Nineveh low.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the claim to be without rival as a claim belonging to God alone. Both traditions compare Isaiah 47:8 by reference, and they name Nahum’s message about Nineveh alongside this verse without harmonizing the two.
